title: Print with the stamps you have
allegory: Tokenizing is printing text with a fixed box of rubber stamps: common chunks have their own numbered stamp, rare words are spelled from several small ones, and the space before a word is carved onto the same stamp.
map: the token id the model actually reads
a rare word spelled with several small stamps
a string split into several tokens, like 'R' + 'alph'
the space carved onto the front of a stamp
the leading space folded into the token: ' Mary' and 'Mary' are different ids
stamps carved but never practised with
glitch tokens whose embeddings were barely trained
credit: The 'so much LLM weirdness is really tokenization' framing (arithmetic, trailing spaces, SolidGoldMagikarp) is Andrej Karpathy's, from 'Let's build the GPT Tokenizer'.

chapters.name: The weird split
chapters.note: that is not where I would cut it

cap.1: You type 56873+3184623. The model never sees your digits one by one. It sees six chunks: 568, 73, +, 318, 46, 23. Nobody would cut it there.
cap.2: Models read token ids, not characters. GPT-2 splits '56873+3184623' into '568', '73', '+', '318', '46', '23', a large part of why small models are bad at arithmetic.
cap.3: Input is a sequence of ids from a fixed BPE vocabulary. The segmentation is a by-product of merge statistics, not meaning, so digit groupings are arbitrary.

cap.1: Picture printing with a box of rubber stamps. Common chunks have their own stamp; a rarer word is spelled with several small ones. Every stamp has a number.
cap.2: A tokenizer is a fixed vocabulary: each stamp is a token with an integer id. Common strings get one token; rare ones are built from several smaller tokens.
cap.3: A tokenizer deterministically maps strings to id sequences over a fixed vocabulary; the ids then index rows of W_E. Nothing about meaning enters at this stage.

parts.note: repeat until the box is full

cap.1: Nobody designs the stamps by hand. Start with single letters, glue together the pair seen most often, and repeat until the box is full.
cap.2: Byte-pair encoding starts from single bytes and keeps merging the most frequent adjacent pair into a new token until the vocabulary is full. You will call it, never write it.
cap.3: BPE fits a merge list greedily on a corpus, from bytes up to a target vocabulary size, and encoding replays those merges. Segmentation mirrors that corpus's statistics, not meaning.

chapters.name: Spaces are carved on
chapters.title: the leading space is part of the stamp

cap.1: The space in front of a word is carved onto the same stamp. ' Ralph' is one stamp. 'Ralph' with no space needs two: R and alph.
cap.2: BPE folds the leading space into the token, so ' Ralph' is one common token while 'Ralph' is 'R' + 'alph'. To the model these are different inputs.
cap.3: Leading-space variants are distinct ids with distinct embeddings, and the space-less variant is often rarer or split. Word identity is not token identity.

chapters.name: The leading-space trap
chapters.verdict: Print the tokens before you trust a number.

cap.1: Ask how much the model prefers Mary over John, but type the name without its space, and you are asking about a different stamp. Nothing warns you.
cap.2: In IOI, GPT-2 must predict ' Mary' with the space. Compare logits for 'Mary' and you measure a different token. Every [1.2] and [1.4] exercise depends on getting this right first.
cap.3: Answer tokens must match the in-context tokenization (' Mary', not 'Mary'); otherwise logit differences, attributions and patching metrics quietly track the wrong ids.

cap.1: Some stamps were carved but hardly ever used while the model practised. Asked to repeat ' SolidGoldMagikarp', GPT-3 said 'distribute'.
cap.2: Rumbelow and Watkins (2023) found a knot of GPT-2 tokens near the centre of its embedding space: common when the vocabulary was built, nearly absent from training.
cap.3: Glitch tokens: BPE merges were fit on one corpus and pretraining ran on another, so those W_E rows got near-zero gradient and stayed near initialisation. Behaviour on them is arbitrary.

chapters.name: Why it matters
items: Never end a prompt with a stray space
The vocabulary is part of the model

cap.1: Every experiment you run on a model starts here. Check the stamps first, or you will measure something other than what you meant.
cap.2: Before any logit difference or patching, print model.to_str_tokens(prompt) on the exact string. Build prompts with explicit leading spaces, and never leave a trailing one.
cap.3: Token identity is the unit of every interp measurement: logit diffs, attention patterns, patch positions. Verify segmentation before you study or steer a model.

caption.1: Drag the merges up from 0. Frequent pairs glue first, and each space glues onto the front of its word. Watch 'Mary' and '␣Mary' become two different stamps.
caption.2: This is BPE learning on one sentence: each merge glues the most frequent adjacent pair. Repeated chunks become single tokens first; rare ones like '␣left' stay in pieces longest.
caption.3: Toy BPE with GPT-2-style pre-splitting: the leading space attaches to its word and merges never cross words. The two Marys end up as unrelated ids, the ' Mary' vs 'Mary' trap.

where_else: Prompt templates: one stray trailing space changes the tokens the model sees
Arithmetic and spelling slips: the model sees chunks, not digits or letters
Interpretability: every logit difference and patch position is keyed to a token
Glitch tokens like ' SolidGoldMagikarp': vocabulary slots the model never learned

hamming.what: Turning text into a sequence of integer ids from a fixed vocabulary of chunks, built by repeatedly merging frequent pairs.
hamming.when: Every time text goes into or comes out of a language model, and first thing in every interpretability experiment.
hamming.why: The model never sees letters, only chunks, so where the cuts fall and whether a space is attached decide what you are actually measuring.

object.title: The stamp row
object.subtitle: The stamps GPT-2 uses to print 56873+3184623, then ' Ralph' and 'Ralph'; each block is as tall as the characters it prints.

cap.1: Nine rubber stamps in a row. Each block is as tall as the number of characters its stamp prints.
cap.2: One block per token. Height = characters in the token.
cap.3: Blocks are tokens; height is string length, a rough proxy for how common the merged chunk was.

cap.1: The first six print 56873+3184623. The cuts fall at 568|73 and 318|46|23, nowhere a person would put them.
cap.2: GPT-2's split of '56873+3184623'. The chunks follow merge frequency, not place value.
cap.3: Digit chunking is inherited from BPE merge statistics, so the same number can split differently in different contexts.

cap.1: Same name, two ways. '␣Ralph' is one tall stamp with the space carved on. 'Ralph' with no space needs two: R and alph.
cap.2: ' Ralph' is one common token; 'Ralph' is 'R' + 'alph'. Different ids, different embeddings.
cap.3: Leading-space variants occupy unrelated rows of W_E; the space-less form here is not even a single token.

cap.1: The model only ever sees the numbers on these stamps. Everything after this works on stamps, never on letters.
cap.2: Attention, the residual stream and sampling all operate on token ids and their embeddings.
cap.3: Tokenization is the only place language becomes integers; every downstream computation is indexed by these ids.

predict.q: Is ' Mary' (with a space) the same token as 'Mary'?
predict.why: BPE folds the leading space into the token, so GPT-2 treats ' Mary' and 'Mary' as different tokens.

options.t: Those chunks were frequent when the vocabulary was built
The model groups digits in threes on purpose

predict.why: BPE merges the most frequent adjacent pairs in its corpus. The cuts follow frequency, not place value.

predict.q: A token was common when the vocabulary was built but almost absent from training. What does the model do with it?

options.t: Something arbitrary: its embedding was barely trained
Treats it like the nearest real word

predict.why: Glitch tokens like ' SolidGoldMagikarp' sat near the centre of embedding space, untouched by training. GPT-3 repeated it as 'distribute'.

object.where: Anywhere text meets a model: prompt templates, few-shot separators, and every token-keyed interpretability measurement.
